units.title: The benchmark question, its decision owner and an immutable manifest
outcomes: Turn a serving benchmark into a decision with an owner, two alternatives and a reversal condition.
Extend your experiment manifest to bind request semantics, quality, failures and cost to each result.
Separate tuning traffic from a frozen final evaluation corpus before selecting configurations.
units.why: Build on Manifests, claim schemas, predictions declared first and artifact lineage. The new contract must support a serving decision, not just reproduce a device timing.

next.note: Choose counters that answer the declared decision.

study.title: The optimization plan before the benchmark
study.locator: Chapter 9, LLM Serving Optimization Plan, printed pp. 294 to 296; Step 2: Generate Benchmark Traffic, pp. 297 to 300
study.depth: Read the workflow, not the hardware setup commands. Replace the worked model and deployment with a small model that fits your GPU; keep distributed variants as reading.

study.title: Bind experiments to their serving contract
study.locator: Core requirements: recorded workload corpus; Architecture constraints: versions, tuning versus final traces and hardware tier; Milestone C: hypothesis and reversal conditions

focus: Name the decision owner and the action the evidence can change: retain the baseline, enable the contribution or add capacity. Set correctness and SLO gates before tuning.
Bind model, tokenizer, template, adapter, weight and KV precision, engine revision, effective configuration, hardware state and workload hashes to the run.
Retain intended arrival times, output limits, stop rules, tenant scope, deadlines, retry policy and quality evaluator. A prompt list alone is not a workload.
Split by sessions or shared-prefix groups where leakage is possible. Freeze final traces and transformations before configuration selection.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write a decision record and manifest for your existing `servelab` baseline. Give each tuning and final corpus a digest. Change the output stop rule in a second record and verify that the workload identity changes rather than silently reusing the first result.
traps: A package version does not identify a locally patched engine. Record the source revision and patch digest too.
Selecting a configuration after inspecting final traces turns them into tuning data. Acquire a new final set before making a generalization claim.
Calling synthetic prefix repetition representative of demand. It isolates reuse; it does not supply production arrival or length distributions.

selfTest.q: What makes a benchmark question actionable?
selfTest.a: An owner, a choice between alternatives, fixed correctness and SLO constraints, and an observation that would reverse the choice.
Tokenization, arrivals, output lengths, stopping, cache state, retries and evaluation can change the work even when prompt text stays fixed.

selfTest.q: May the final workload use the same length distribution as tuning?
selfTest.a: Yes. The distributions can match, but final requests or sessions must not have been used to select the configuration. Record any intended distribution shift separately.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `servelab` decision record, immutable experiment manifests and separate tuning and final traces.
units.stopWhen: Your decision record names two alternatives and a reversal condition, and a changed request contract cannot reuse an old manifest identity.

units.title: Offered and completed load, goodput and useful work
outcomes: Reconcile offered, admitted, completed, failed and pending work from one trace boundary.
Compute request and token goodput under a fixed quality and latency contract.
Explain a utilization increase that does not increase useful completed work.
units.why: Build on Benchmark scenarios, MLPerf boundaries and endpoint goodput. Here you audit the engine's accounting and use it to locate sustainable serving capacity.

next.note: Price useful outputs instead of gross token activity.

study.title: Audit throughput and the traffic boundary
study.locator: Chapter 9, Step 3: Define Evaluation Metrics, printed pp. 300 to 301; Step 5: Benchmark the Qwen3 Model with vLLM, pp. 302 to 303
study.depth: Use the two workload reports as accounting examples, not a controlled cache ablation: their length distributions and request rates differ. Do not infer cache benefit from their total-token throughput ratio.

study.title: Capacity subject to per-request service quality
study.locator: arXiv:2407.07000v2, Sections 2.2, 3.1 and 4.2: metric boundaries, hidden stalls and Capacity Evaluation

focus: Use the same observation interval for rates. Also report an arrival cohort followed to terminal outcomes; a drain interval must not be silently counted as offered-load time.
Define request goodput as quality-accepted completions satisfying all declared request SLOs per second. Token goodput counts only the accepted outputs of those requests, using one tokenizer.
Capacity is a sustainable offered rate satisfying the target success fraction without persistent queue growth. It is not the maximum observed completion rate during a drain.
Device busy time, padding, recomputation and rejected output can increase utilization without increasing useful work. Use correlated request and iteration traces to distinguish them.
units.reproduce: Recount one `servelab` trace closed-book. For a CPU-checkable fixture, offer 100 unique requests in 10 seconds with no initial queue: 70 succeed, 10 fail, 10 are rejected and 10 remain pending at the boundary. Of the successes, 50 pass both quality and SLO gates and each returns 20 accepted output tokens. Obtain 10 offered requests/s, 7 successful completions/s, 5 good requests/s and 100 good output tokens/s; account for every request once.
traps: Calling the configured request rate the actual offered rate when client concurrency limits delay sending. Retain intended and actual send times.
Counting cached input tokens as executed prefill work. Logical input throughput and computed-token throughput need separate counters.
Dropping timeouts from the denominator. They are demand and service failures, not missing observations.

selfTest.q: Can completed load briefly exceed offered load?
selfTest.a: Yes, when an earlier backlog drains. Report the initial and final backlog and use a common time boundary.

selfTest.q: Does higher device utilization prove a useful throughput gain?
selfTest.a: No. Padding, retries or recomputation can keep the device busy. Valid accepted completions and their SLOs determine useful work.

selfTest.q: Is request goodput multiplied by mean output length always token goodput?
selfTest.a: Only if that mean is taken over the same good requests with the same tokenizer and interval. A mean over all completions can give a different value.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `servelab` raw-outcome reconciliation and offered-load sweep with quality- and SLO-aware goodput.
units.stopWhen: Every offered request is accounted for, and you identify a sustainable load point from success fraction, goodput and queue growth rather than utilization alone.

fit.note: Chapter 9 supplies accounting examples and Etalon supplies the constrained capacity workflow; the mini-project supplies measurement and reconciliation.

units.title: Cost per token, quality acceptance, retry cost and energy
outcomes: Derive input, output and quality-accepted output unit costs with explicit allocation rules.
Account for failed attempts, retries, idle capacity and failure reserve in serving cost.
Optionally derive joules and operational carbon per useful output with an explicit measurement boundary.
units.why: Build on Unit cost, headroom and simpler designs. Token counts now need quality, retry and allocation rules before they can support an economic comparison.

next.note: Carry attempt cost and useful-output rates into the capacity plan.

study.title: Quality, retries and cost belong to one planner
study.locator: Core requirements: analytical planner; Architecture constraints: correctness and quality; Failure-injection requirements: retry storm; Measurement requirements: quality and cost/token/request

study.title: Optional energy and operational carbon boundary
study.locator: Energy measurement techniques: Hardware power counters and System-level energy profiling; Carbon Footprint Calculation: Operational carbon calculation, equation 11
study.depth: Optional: read the measurement and unit-conversion method only. Do not adopt the chapter's hardware power estimates or fleet results.

focus: For total interval cost \(C\), report \(C/N_{\text{in}}\), \(C/N_{\text{out}}\) and \(C/N_{\text{accepted}}\) as separate normalizations, not additive charges. Splitting input and output charges requires an explicit allocation policy.
Sum costs over every attempt for a logical request; count its accepted output once. Retry amplification depends on failure correlation, backoff, deadline and attempt cap.
Keep quality acceptance separate from speculative draft-token acceptance. A verified draft token is not evidence that an answer meets the application's quality gate.
Optional: integrate measured power over the same interval as accepted work. GPU energy alone is not total IT energy; facility overhead and grid intensity are assumptions unless measured.
units.reproduce: Derive a synthetic accounting example without notes: an interval costs 12 currency units, processes 6000 input tokens and generates 3000 output tokens across all attempts, of which 2000 are quality-accepted useful output tokens. Obtain 0.002 per input token, 0.004 per generated output token and 0.006 per accepted token. With independent attempts of constant cost \(c\), success probability \(p\) and unlimited retries, derive expected cost \(c/p\); state why bounded deadlines and correlated failures require a different model. Optional: a constant 100 W over 10 seconds is 1000 J, or 0.5 J per accepted token for this fixture.
traps: Dividing only successful-attempt cost by accepted output. Failed attempts and provisioned idle time still consume budget.
Comparing token costs across tokenizers as if tokens were identical work. Use the same text tasks and quality gate; report tokenizer identity.
Applying facility overhead twice or to GPU energy alone and calling it a measured facility footprint. State what is missing.

selfTest.q: May input-normalized and output-normalized total costs be added?
selfTest.a: No. Each uses the same numerator. Adding them double counts cost; additive input/output prices need an allocation or billing rule.

selfTest.q: When does expected retry cost equal \(c/p\)?
selfTest.a: For independent, identically distributed attempts, constant per-attempt cost, positive success probability and unlimited retries. Deadline caps and correlated failures invalidate that shortcut.

selfTest.q: What if no output passes the quality gate?
selfTest.a: Cost per accepted token has no finite value. Report zero accepted output and the spent cost; do not replace the denominator with generated tokens.

selfTest.q: How do you convert energy to operational carbon?
selfTest.a: Multiply facility energy in kWh by the corresponding grid intensity in mass per kWh. Apply facility overhead once if starting from complete IT energy; report embodied carbon separately.

units.stopWhen: Your cost table reconciles all attempts and idle/reserve charges, counts accepted work once and states the units and allocation boundary of every denominator.
